name: Karl Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Holt Motors on Mill Road by half seven, kettle on, then whatever's on the board. Dennis, the owner, takes the bookings on paper and I do the work: clutches, brakes, exhausts, a lot of older hatchbacks people keep running because they can't afford new. I like the moment a car that came in limping drives out quiet. What wears me out is the cold in winter and lying on the creeper with rust dropping in my eyes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and what's the place like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nine years, since I was eighteen and doing my certificate. It's two bays, me, Dennis and a lad called Rory who's on his first year. The pay is low for what we do, and I've got less than a month's rent put by, but Dennis has always been fair with me, so I stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Honestly that's what I'd expect anyway. The software in our diagnostic box hasn't changed much in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've always said: you can't fix a seized bolt with an app. Down the pub I'd be the one laughing at the adverts. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something about the tech bosses getting it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI was never my big worry. My big worry is Dennis. He's sixty-three and he's talked about selling up, and there's only one other garage within twenty minutes, and they've got their own lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep turning up and keep my head down, same as now. I'd try to put fifty a month aside, though it never quite survives the car insurance month. Nadia, my girlfriend, and I talked about joining the union at her care home's sister branch for trades, so I might actually sign up this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for about a day, and then the usual knot comes back. Nothing about AI fixes the rent going up or my boss Dennis wanting to retire. It's the same tired feeling, just without a new monster in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Dennis selling. What happens to you if he does?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a chain buys the unit, maybe they keep me on a worse contract, maybe they bring their own people. If it becomes flats, I'm driving forty minutes to the city every day on a car that's older than Rory. I'd rather not think about it, which is probably the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first if money gets tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, then the phone upgrade I've been promising myself. After that it's the van fund, which is a joke because there's barely anything in it. Rent and Nadia's half of the shopping are the two things I won't touch.

say: AI was **mostly hype** and a scan tool can't free a seized bolt.
The **tech bosses** oversold it, and working people were right to doubt them.
think: My real worry is **Dennis selling** the garage, not software.
There are **few garages** nearby, so losing this job means a long commute or worse.
do: Keep **turning up** at Holt Motors and keep my head down.
Try to save **fifty a month**, though insurance month usually eats it.
Sign up to a **trades union** branch this year, like Nadia suggested.
feel: **Relieved** briefly, then the old knot about rent and Dennis returns.
S0.quote: Nothing about AI fixes the rent going up or my boss Dennis wanting to retire.
fieldNote: Karl's **existing worry** is the garage owner's retirement, which AI Plateau doesn't touch.
Resistant to tech, he treats the **plateau** as proof he was right all along.
Union talk comes from his **girlfriend**, and he seems half committed to it.

steps.text: Keep working the two bays at Holt Motors as normal
Put fifty a month into savings outside insurance month
Join a trades union branch before the end of the year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds more like what's actually happening. The parts suppliers are already pushing apps at Dennis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the paperwork side of the trade gets eaten and the spanner side stays. I'd be telling people at the pub that it's the office jobs who should worry, not us. Online I'd share the union stuff about protecting workers when firms bring this in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the thinking bits of my day are bigger than I let on. Fault-finding, looking up torque specs, ordering parts, writing the job card. If a chain buys Holt's and puts a tablet in every bay, they'll want one fewer mechanic who's quick with it, and that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ask Dennis straight out what his plans are, because I've been avoiding that talk. I'd get Rory to show me the parts app on his phone, even though I hate it. And I'd keep the union card and actually go to a meeting about how garages use this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, if I'm honest. I'm not old enough to be past it and not young enough to start again cheaply. It's that in-between bit that makes me cross.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rory, oddly. He's quick on the tablet but he can't feel a bad wheel bearing through the steering yet, and if the computer does the thinking he may never learn. And Dennis, because he'd have to buy all the new kit or sell, and he can't afford the kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the spanner side stays, but you also think you'd lose out. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. The spanner side stays, but there's less of it per mechanic once the computer does the diagnosis in two minutes. So two mechanics' worth of spannering might become one and a half, and I know which half I'd be.

say: AI takes the **paperwork side**, and hands-on mechanics like us stay safe.
Firms bringing in AI need **union rules** to protect the people on the tools.
think: **Fault-finding**, specs and parts ordering are a bigger slice of my day than I admit.
A chain with tablets in every bay would keep **one fewer mechanic**, probably not me.
do: Ask **Dennis directly** about selling, instead of avoiding the conversation.
Get Rory to teach me the **parts app**, even though I hate it.
Attend a **union meeting** on how garages are using AI.
feel: **Tight** in the chest and cross about being caught in between.
S1.quote: Two mechanics' worth of spannering might become one and a half, and I know which half I'd be.
fieldNote: Gap between **say** and **think**: publicly the tools are safe, privately he fears the diagnosis shift.
He frames the threat as **fewer hours** spread across fewer mechanics, not a robot replacing him.
Worry for the **apprentice** Rory shows real care for how the trade gets learned.

steps.text: Ask Rory to show him the parts-ordering app on his phone
Go to a union meeting about AI in garages
Ask Dennis about selling, then wait to see the answer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's next winter and the one after. That's not a plan, that's a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in, full stop. Out loud I'd be saying tax the companies that make the robots and pay people while they work out what's next. I'd share every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the first two years it's the thinking that goes: the diagnosis, the quotes, the ordering, maybe Dennis's whole booking book. My hands keep me in work till about 2031, then the robots come for the bays. So I'd get three years of being the hands for a computer, then nothing, and I'd be thirty-two with no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, I'd pay off the bit left on the car and stop the van fund, because there's no point dreaming of my own van. I'd go to every union meeting going and push for redundancy terms. In the first year after it arrives I'd look at jobs where people still want a human, like Nadia's care work, even though it pays worse than this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like the moment a lift slips an inch with a car on it. I'd be lying awake doing sums that don't add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Nadia that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Nadia that her care job is probably safer than mine now, which would be strange for both of us. Then we'd sit at the kitchen table and work out whether we can live on her wage for a bit. I don't think we could, not with the rent at nine hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me time, but time for what? I'm not good with screens, so I can't move into the computer side. Mostly it's three years to watch it coming and save what I can, which isn't much on my pay.

say: The **government** must tax robot makers and pay people while they adjust.
Two years is **a cliff**, not a plan, and I'd sign every petition.
think: Diagnosis, quotes and **booking** go by 2028, and the bays go around **2031**.
I'd be **thirty-two** with no savings once robots reach the bays.
do: Pay off the **car loan** and drop the van fund straight away.
Push for **redundancy terms** at every union meeting.
Look at **care work** in the first year, like Nadia's, despite lower pay.
feel: **Sick**, like a lift slipping with a car on it.
Lying awake doing **sums** that don't add up.
S2.quote: My hands keep me in work till about 2031, then the robots come for the bays.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** feels like a waiting room to Karl, not a runway.
He can't see himself moving into **screen work**, so the extra time buys little.
His **girlfriend's care job** becomes the household's safer income, which unsettles him.

steps.text: Pay off the last of the car loan this year
Push for redundancy terms at every union meeting
Sign petitions to tax robot makers and fund wage support
Apply for care work jobs like Nadia's in the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast, but at least you can see it in the mirror before it hits you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing as before, but louder, because there'd be time to organise. I'd be telling the lads at the trade counter to join the union now, not when the letters come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully it means 2031 for the thinking side and 2034 for my hands. I'd be thirty-five then. That's eight years of work, maybe, if Dennis doesn't sell first, but I'd have nothing to show for it unless something changes now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the college and ask what the cheapest course is that leads somewhere robots can't easily go, maybe heating engineering or electrics in old houses. I'd do it two nights a week. I'd also get serious about the union and try to get the garages in town to sign something about notice and retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than sick this time. Five years is like knowing the cambelt's due: you can drive on it for a while, but you know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you prefer the familiar. How would you really feel about going back to college?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate the first month, sitting in a classroom at twenty-eight with eighteen-year-olds. But I did it once at sixteen and I came out with a trade. If there's five years, I'd rather be the one who started early than the one who waited, even though waiting is what I usually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course fee, if there's no grant, and two evenings a week away from Nadia. We'd skip the holiday we were planning for next summer. I'd want the union or the government to cover the fee, honestly, because I haven't got it.

say: Five years is **time to organise**, so mechanics should join the union now.
Garages should sign up to **notice and retraining** money before the letters come.
think: Thinking work goes in **2031**, my hands in **2034**, when I'm thirty-five.
Without a change now, those **eight years** leave me with nothing to show.
do: Ask the **college** about a cheap heating or electrics course.
Study **two nights** a week alongside the garage job.
Push town garages to sign a **retraining** agreement through the union.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than sick, like driving on a cambelt that's due.
S3.quote: Five years is like knowing the cambelt's due: you can drive on it for a while, but you know.
fieldNote: Five years moves Karl from **waiting** to grudging action, against his own habit.
He picks trades like **heating and electrics** in old houses as safer from robots.
He expects **public or union money** to fund retraining he can't afford.

steps.text: Enrol in a heating or electrics evening course at the college
Get town garages to sign a union retraining agreement
Skip next summer's holiday to cover the course fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven before the robots reach the bays. That's a whole other life away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse for governments not to have a plan. I'd want free retraining written into law, and I'd say so to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is the one where I'd probably do nothing for too long. I know myself. I'd think there's loads of time, and then it'd be 2034 and I'd still be under the same hatchback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set myself a rule: start a course within two years, not ten. I'd stay at Holt's and try to save properly, maybe a hundred a month once the car's paid off. And I'd keep going to the union so that when it does come, there's something in place for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, but there's guilt in it, because I know I'll put it off. It's a slow worry instead of a fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might push you to actually start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia, probably. She's the one who does the planning in our house. If she put the college leaflet on the fridge, I'd feel it every time I got the milk out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the ten years change anything about having a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might. We've said maybe kids around thirty. With ten years, I'd feel all right about that, as long as I'm on a path to something by then. With two years I'd have said no straight away.

say: A decade means **no excuse** for governments to lack a plan.
**Free retraining** should be written into law for mechanics and trades.
think: Ten years is when I'd **put it off** for too long.
I could still be under the **same hatchback** in 2034.
do: Set a rule to **start a course** within two years.
Save a **hundred a month** once the car loan is cleared.
Keep going to **union meetings** so protections exist when it arrives.
feel: **Calmer**, but with guilt about knowing I'll delay.
A **slow worry** instead of a fast one.
S4.quote: I'd think there's loads of time, and then it'd be 2034 and I'd still be under the same hatchback.
fieldNote: Karl is **honest** that more time may make him act later, not sooner.
His thin cushion and **low pay** keep him anxious even with a decade.
**Family plans** around thirty depend on having a path, which he links to time.

steps.text: Start a college course within two years of hearing
Save a hundred a month after the car loan ends
Keep attending union meetings about AI in trades
Plan children around thirty only once a new path is set

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. Three years of being a computer's hands and then the robots, with nothing saved and nothing else I'm good at. What would help is someone paying me while I learn a trade robots can't easily do, and a rule that garages have to give proper notice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cars. People round here drive old cars because they're skint, and nobody's going to sell them a robot service. I think garages like Holt's will be the last to change, and I don't know if that's my luck or my trap.

headlineQuote: I'm not old enough to be past it and not young enough to start again cheaply.
portrait: Karl, 27, has spent **nine years** at a two-bay garage, fixing older cars for people who can't afford new.
He has **less than a month** saved and worries most about his boss retiring and selling.
He **avoids technology** and sees the AI hype as overblown, though privately fears losing diagnosis work.
In the AGI pictures he wants **unions and government** to fund retraining he can't afford himself.
He admits more time might make him **delay**, and leans on his girlfriend Nadia to push him.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving him a computer's hands for three years, then replaced, with no savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** into a trade robots can't easily do.
A rule forcing garages to give **proper notice**.
